_README: Source names removed from approach_variants — the column my prose sweep did not cover, found when
one of these variants turned out to name a climbing site outright. 5 routes of the 675 carrying
variants; every one predates the no-sources rule being applied to this column.
Each edit is an exact substring replacement asserted to match exactly once against the live text.

approach_variants.name: Cathedral Pass, the gear-cache trees, and the traverse to the original route's first pitch
approach_variants.notes:
Drive and hike as for the Northeast Buttress: Trail #1345 from the Cathedral Rock trailhead at about 3,350 ft, past Nosh Nosh Wahtum at 2.5 miles, to Cathedral Pass and the PCT junction at 5,550 ft and 4 miles. Sign the wilderness permit at the register.

Cut across the meadow to the stand of trees — the usual gear cache — and traverse under the east face across talus to the northeast side.

This variation does not have its own start on the ground: it begins where the ORIGINAL Northeast Ridge route finishes its first pitch.

About 6.4 km and 3,400 ft.
approach_variants.season: Late July to September. Late August and September give the driest rock and the coldest, most stable air, which is worth waiting for where the protection is already marginal
hazards: Shattered, friable andesite giving loose holds and unreliable protection
An explicitly unstable class 4+ section low on the route that must be crossed to reach the good climbing
PG13 protection with significant fall consequences
Rockfall onto belayers from a ridge littered with loose blocks
Six pitches at 5.9 plus a route-finding descent make benightment a real risk on a short day
No cell coverage and a remote gravel-access trailhead: slow rescue
approach_variants.baseFinding:
BE CLEAR ABOUT WHAT YOU ARE LOOKING FOR: THIS ROUTE'S BASE IS THE TOP OF SOMEBODY ELSE'S FIRST PITCH. You find the original Northeast Ridge start — the short steep snowfield on the northeast side, exiting LEFT into the moat rather than right onto the harder ledges — climb its first pitch, and only then are you at the beginning of the 2003 line.

THE FEATURE THAT PROVES YOU ARE ON THE VARIATION AND NOT ON THE ORIGINAL, and this is the one to memorise, is YELLOW-SPECKLED ROCK. From the top of that first pitch, traverse LEFT and up over a short pitch of genuinely unstable class 4+ ground, aiming for a LEFT-HAND VERTICAL CRACK in a LEFT-FACING CORNER, identified by yellow-speckled rock with ROOFS ABOVE IT. Yellow speckles plus roofs above a left-facing corner is the target; nothing else on this side of the peak reads that way.

THE CONFIRMATION IS THE THIRD PITCH: it climbs that crack and exits over its LEFT side. It is the best pitch on the route, 5.7 to 5.8 and well protected — which is worth knowing precisely because everything below it is not. If pitch three is poorly protected choss, you are not in the corner you wanted.

A HIGHER CHECK: above, the rock eases, and a short difficult LEFT-LEANING CRACK at 5.9+ comes before moderate terrain to the summit.

AND THE HONEST WARNING THAT BELONGS IN A BASE FINDING HERE: the pitch you must cross to reach the good climbing is described by the first-ascent party as scary and unstable. It is rated PG13, and the route would carry more stars if not for that second pitch. Knowing that in advance is what stops a party assuming they are off route when the ground feels wrong.

approach_variants.name: PCT to Red Pass, then the climbers' path up to the saddle
approach_variants.notes:
From the PCT trailhead at exit 52, hike the PCT north about two miles to the Commonwealth Creek / Red Mountain Trail #1033 junction. Follow that trail, crossing Commonwealth Creek, roughly 1.7 miles further, passing Red Mountain on your right and Red Pond on your left, to the Red Mountain Saddle — Red Pass — at about 5,320 ft. The old PCT dropped from here toward Goldmyer Hot Springs.

From the saddle, follow a winding climbers' path up to the base of the route. Allow about two hours for the approach from the trailhead, more if there is snow.

This is a short technical add-on for parties already scrambling in the Red Pass and Commonwealth Basin area, not a day out on its own.
approach_variants.season: Mid-summer into early autumn, once the Red Pass approach and the rock are dry
hazards: Loose, fractured red rock along this ridge system, more pronounced than on the south face
Short but real exposure on the summit block
Possible steep snow on the contour across the northeast side of the second false summit in early or late season
Aging fixed bolts of unknown provenance as the only in-situ protection
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THREE OVERSIZED BOLTS ARE THE PROOF, AND THEY ARE THE REASON THIS ROUTE IS FINDABLE AT ALL. The pitch carries THREE fixed bolts, described by everyone who has climbed it as monstrous — large enough that they make the route-finding non-adventurous. If you are on a 30 m pitch of broken rock with three big bolts in it, you are on this route. If you cannot see a bolt, you are on the ridge somewhere else.

WHAT THE PITCH IS: a very short 30 m lead, broken rock, past a SLAB SECTION and then a small section of more featured rock to the top. There are many variations and they are all easy. So the difficulty will not identify it; the hardware will.

HOW TO GET TO IT FROM THE SADDLE, AND THE ONE THING TO KEEP STRAIGHT: from Red Pass the climbers' path winds WEST and up. Passing Red Mountain on your right and Red Pond on your left on the way in is the confirmation you are approaching the pass from the correct side.

A NAMING WARNING THAT COULD SEND YOU TO ANOTHER MOUNTAIN, AND IT IS A REAL ONE: the published location text for this route refers to a saddle between Lundin and East Lundin peaks, while the approach it gives goes to Red Pass and then west, which is Red Mountain's ground rather than Lundin's. TWO different published descriptions both called East Ridge exist on Red Mountain — one describing this saddle-to-summit line over two false summits, and one describing a ridge traverse from Point 5720 near the Kendall Katwalk, which its own author recommends nobody repeat. Three descriptions, one name. Fix the peak by the saddle and the three bolts, not by the route name.

IF YOU CONTINUE OVER THE FALSE SUMMITS toward the main peak, the sequence from the Red Mountain Saddle is: up the southeast side of the first false summit, a 30 ft class 3 gully down at its northwest end, right (north) to the big notch, 50 ft up slabs on the far side, a contour across the heathery northeast side of the second false summit, over that summit, then 100 ft of class 3 down a moderate gully to the final notch at about 5,840 ft below the main summit.

approach_variants.name: Phelps Creek and Leroy Basin, over the col and across the Gloomy Glacier
approach_variants.notes:
Same walk in as for Seven Fingered Jack and Maude: Phelps Creek trail to the Leroy Creek crossing at about 4,140 ft, then the steep unmaintained climbers' trail on the north side of the creek into Leroy Basin at about 6,100 ft.

This is the common approach but not the elegant one. It exists because the alternative is the ferry up Lake Chelan to Holden and the Railroad Creek trail into Copper Basin, which gains the East Ridge — the standard route — much more directly. A third option starts at Cottonwood on the Entiat River and reaches the East Ridge by way of the Entiat Glacier. All three converge on the same south-east face finish.

From Leroy Basin, head north-west toward a waterfall and climb its left side to a small notch on the ridge of Seven Fingered Jack. Published descriptions of this saddle vary — one places it just west of an obvious 7,700 ft col with a couple of bivy sites at the low point, another gives it as a notch reached past a second creek crossing — and they may or may not be the same feature, so check it on a map rather than assuming.

From the saddle you must DROP about a thousand feet into the moraine at the terminus of the Gloomy Glacier, and every foot of it has to be regained on the way out. Two published ways down: descend to the tarn below and go around a prominent rock formation that guards the basin, or descend to the right across sandy ledges and down large boulders.

Expect roughly nine hours round trip from Leroy Basin, and a very long day car to car — one party left the trailhead at three in the morning and got back at eleven at night.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep; the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing runs through avalanche terrain earlier than that
hazards: A thousand feet of descent into the Gloomy basin that must be regained on the way out
Avalanche terrain on the Leroy-to-Gloomy crossing
Icy forty-degree slopes near the top of the Gloomy Glacier, with crevasses below the usual line
Two thousand feet of exceptionally loose talus and scree above the basin
The narrow exposed ledge traverse off the col, which is avoidable and should be avoided
Route-finding is the crux — this is regarded as the most complex of the three Entiat nine-thousanders
approach_variants.baseFinding:
FERNOW IS NOT VISIBLE FROM LEROY BASIN, and this is confirmed rather than folklore. Parties climbing the basin under the cirque of Seven Fingered Jack report having real difficulty identifying the route because the peak simply is not in view. Do not stand in the basin trying to pick your line off the mountain; you cannot see it. Carry a track.

The arrival test is short and physical: cross the moraine below the Gloomy Glacier, go UP THE WATERFALL, and you are in the broad basin below Fernow. That is where the climbing starts.

Above that basin there are two decision points and both have a wrong answer that is on record.

FIRST: descend the glacier to its terminal moraine at about 6,500 ft, then climb the RIGHT side of a stream to an upper snow-filled basin, and from there go south-west up a broad gully that turns eastward. That is Class 2-3 and gives you the luxury of knowing where you are. The alternative — dropping only to 7,000 ft and making a rising traverse through a succession of gullies, ribs and small cliffs — is Class 3-plus with snow and ice and the feeling of being lost somewhere in the Entiat Mountains.

SECOND, and this is the one that matters: from the broad gully, DO NOT go all the way to the col and traverse the south-east face on the narrow ledges there. They are described as exposed enough to frighten a bird, with the honest observation that a fallen body would be unlikely to be found. Instead climb the broad gully to about 8,400 ft, then a loose gully to about 9,000 ft, and traverse the face at NINE THOUSAND on a wide ledge that is not exposed at all.

The 8,400 ft mark is a real landmark rather than a number on a map — two independent parties record the ground changing character there, one of them at a large bench holding permanent snow with water running off it. From 8,400 the line goes up loose talus to the ridge between Seven Fingered Jack and Fernow, where cairns pick up and weave around to the south-east ridge of the summit block. The cairns are reported by three separate parties, though one notes they stop near the summit itself.

The general principle behind all of it: climb as far as you can up the ridge separating Fernow's south-east and south-west faces. Once on the East Ridge, a couple of hundred feet of Class 3 on reasonably solid rock finishes it.

approach_variants.name: South Fork Skokomish Trail #873 to Sundown Pass, then the Six Ridge crest and the Mount Olson Way
approach_variants.notes:
Mount Olson sees very few ascents and is normally reached as a side trip off the long Six Ridge traverse. From the Upper South Fork Skokomish Trailhead (Trail #873), reached via Skokomish Valley Road, FS-23 and FS-2361 from Shelton — FS-2361 is gated 1 October to 30 April — the trail runs up the valley. There is an unbridged FORD of the South Fork at about 2.4 miles and 1,450 ft that is only ankle-deep and safely crossable in late summer or early autumn low water; at other times it is a serious hazard. The Olympic National Park boundary comes near 5.1 miles, after which tread grows fainter and a self-issue backcountry permit is required.

Sundown Pass, a forested saddle marked by a broken signpost, comes at about 7.2 miles and 4,125 ft — this is the junction with the Six Ridge Trail heading east along the crest. Lake Sundown is a short spur off the pass at about 7.6 miles and 4,030 ft: the last dependable water and the standard basecamp.

Follow the Six Ridge Trail east along its sawtooth crest — a ridge either side with a gully in the middle, and brutal uphill for every downhill — to about 8.7 miles and 4,650 ft, where an unsigned, unofficial boot path known as the MOUNT OLSON WAY leaves the trail for the peak. It is faint and overgrown with blowdown and lingering snowfields into midsummer. A boulder-field tarn at about 5,100 ft below the summit block is the last water and a common bivy.
approach_variants.season: Roughly Jul-Sep, and gated by two fords that are only reliably safe in late summer and early autumn low water
hazards: Two unbridged fords only safely crossable in late summer and early autumn low water
Route-finding on trail-less and boot-path terrain with an unsigned departure from Six Ridge
Dense brush and blowdown along the Six Ridge approach
A 55-60 degree grass and heather summit pitch that is loose and exposed, and worse descending
FS-2361 is gated 1 October to 30 April
Afternoon weather on an exposed crest, and a multi-day return from a very lightly visited peak
approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE BASE OF THE CLIMB IS THE PASS IMMEDIATELY EAST OF THE SUMMIT, AND THE TEST IS THAT THE CLIMBING STARTS THE MOMENT YOU STAND IN IT. From the pass, the final ascent to Olson's 5,289 ft top is a steep, unmarked scramble up a GRASSY AND HEATHER SLOPE pitched around 55-60 degrees in places — hands-on, solid Class 3 — directly above you. Grass and heather at that angle is a distinctive surface: it is neither talus nor rock, and you are either on it or you are not.

SECOND TEST, and it is what tells you the slope is easing correctly rather than that you have wandered: the pitch EASES AND CURVES ROUND THE NORTH SIDE of the peak onto a HEATHER BENCH, and then it is an easy stroll to the true summit. So the sequence is steep grass, then a bench that takes you leftward round the peak, then a walk. If the ground stays steep all the way to a top, or if you are on rock and scree rather than heather, you are on the wrong side.

THE APPROACH TEST BEFORE ANY OF THAT is the departure from Six Ridge, because it is the thing people miss: the Mount Olson Way leaves the Six Ridge Trail at the point on the sawtooth crest CLOSEST TO OLSON, at about 4,650 ft, and it is UNSIGNED. It is faint, overgrown and blowdown-choked. If you are still on obvious trail after passing the point where the crest is nearest the peak, you have walked past the turn.

HONEST LIMIT: there is no documented roped climbing route, rack or pitch-by-pitch description for this peak. It is recorded as a summit without a route write-up. This is a bushwhack and scramble objective for peak-baggers, and the markers above are the sum of what has been written down. Treat the notch and the upper summit meadow as the crux going both ways: both are loose and exposed and better handled with an axe or a pole for self-arrest, especially wet or under late snow.

approach_variants.name: PCT to Commonwealth Creek, then cross-country into the cirque
approach_variants.notes:
Identical to the standard South Face approach. Snoqualmie Pass PCT-North trailhead (about 3,000 ft), PCT northbound roughly 2.5 miles to the Commonwealth Creek Trail (#1033) junction, then #1033 into Commonwealth Basin.

Shortly after the trail crosses Commonwealth Creek — the last water — leave the tread, either right there or after the path has begun to swing up onto Red Mountain's flank, and climb cross-country northwest into the upper basin beneath Lundin's south face.

Expect the same talus and boulder travel, and the same lingering early-season snow in the basin, as the standard route.
hazards: Commonwealth Creek ford in early season high flow
no trail beyond the creek crossing
lingering early-season snow in the upper basin
published route topos disagree on where the line starts
approach_variants.baseFinding:
This variation starts near the CENTRE and lowest point of the face, at an obvious layback hand-sized crack. The crack is the identifier, not the position — look for the feature itself.

This matters more here than on most routes: the variation does not start where the original South Face line starts, so a party trying to match an old topo photo will be put in the wrong place. Find the layback crack near the low centre of the face and start there.

If you are on rock with no single obvious crack line, or the crack you have found is off toward one edge of the face rather than near its centre, keep looking along the base rather than committing.
